title: Where is the post office?
goal: Ask for and give directions, use prepositions of place, and form commands.
bekal: ask for directions politely and understand the answer
form commands: the bare stem without *-r*
wave: Review **unit 9** first: describe your day from waking up to going to bed in ten sentences, and start five of them with a time expression — remember to swap the subject and verb.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Undskyld, jeg er faret vild
dialogs.intro: Budi is lost in Aarhus and asks a woman at a bus stop for help.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Undskyld, kan du hjælpe mig? Jeg er faret vild.
lines.id: Excuse me, can you help me? I'm lost.
lines.literal: sorry, can you help me? I am gone wild.

lines.speaker: Kvinden:
lines.id: Of course. Where are you going?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jeg leder efter posthuset. Ligger det langt herfra?
lines.id: I'm looking for the post office. Is it far from here?
lines.literal: I search after post-house-the. lies it far from-here?

lines.speaker: Kvinden:
lines.text: Nej, kun fem minutter. Gå ligeud til lyskrydset.
lines.id: No, only five minutes. Go straight ahead to the traffic lights.
lines.literal: no, only five minutes. walk straight-out to light-crossing-the.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: To the traffic lights. And then?

lines.speaker: Kvinden:
lines.text: Så drejer du til højre ad Nørregade.
lines.id: Then you turn right onto Nørregade.
lines.literal: then turn you to right along Nørregade.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Til højre. Er det den gade med kirken?
lines.id: Right. Is that the street with the church?
lines.literal: to right. is it the street with church-the?

lines.speaker: Kvinden:
lines.text: Præcis. Posthuset ligger lige over for kirken.
lines.id: Exactly. The post office is right across from the church.
lines.literal: precisely. post-house-the lies just over for church-the.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ved siden af hvad? Der er så mange bygninger.
lines.id: Next to what? There are so many buildings.
lines.literal: by side-the of what? there are so many buildings.

lines.speaker: Kvinden:
lines.text: Mellem apoteket og en bank. Du kan ikke overse det — det er rødt.
lines.id: Between the pharmacy and a bank. You can't miss it — it's red.
lines.literal: between pharmacy-the and a bank. you can not oversee it — it is red.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Thanks so much for your help!

lines.speaker: Kvinden:
lines.text: Det var så lidt. Held og lykke!
lines.literal: it was so little. luck and happiness!

notes: **Hvor skal du hen?** = "where are you going?" Notice *hen* at the end — Danish marks **direction** with a small word at the end of the sentence. Compare *Hvor er du?* (where are you — place) with *Hvor skal du hen?* (where are you going — direction), just like old English "where" vs "whither".
**Jeg er faret vild** = I'm lost, literally "I have gone wild". One of those phrases you learn whole; breaking it into parts doesn't help.
**At lede efter** = to look for. *Efter* is required; *jeg leder posthuset* means nothing. There's also *at søge*, which is more formal and used for searching for a job or online.

**At ligge** = to be located, for things that don't move and for buildings. Danish picks the verb by the object's shape: *at ligge* (lie, for flat things), *at stå* (stand, for upright things), *at sidde* (sit, for things attached). *Bogen ligger på bordet*, but *flasken står på bordet*.
**Ad** is used for movement along something: *ad Nørregade* = along Nørregade. A small preposition rarely taught but often heard in directions.
**Lige over for** = right across from. *Lige* strengthens to "right, exactly" — compare *lige her* (right here), *lige nu* (right now).
**Det var så lidt** is the standard reply to thanks, literally "that was so little". Compare *selv tak*. Both are equally common.
**Held og lykke** = good luck. Said before an exam, an interview, or anything that needs a bit of luck.

grammars.title: Commands: the bare stem
body: One of the easiest forms in Danish. Take the infinitive, drop *at*, drop the final *-e* if there is one — and that's your command.
after: Reflexive verbs keep their pronoun, and it matches the listener: *sæt dig!* (one person), *sæt jer!* (several people), *skynd dig!* (hurry up!).
Negative commands: *ikke* comes after the verb — *Kom ikke for sent!*, *Glem det ikke!*

⚠️ Danish commands sound blunter than English ones without "please". For everyday requests, Danes usually ask a question instead: *Kan du lukke døren?* is far more common than *Luk døren!* Bare commands are used for directions, recipes, signs and emergencies.

grammars.title: Prepositions of place
body: This part isn't hard to understand but it is hard to guess, because the choice often seems illogical and has to be learned phrase by phrase.

head: Preposition
Basic meaning
Example
rows: i huset, i bilen, i Danmark, i København
på bordet, på gaden, **på hotellet**, **på arbejde**
til Aarhus, til lyskrydset, til højre
ved døren, ved siden af banken

after: ⚠️ **på** for public places is the biggest surprise for beginners: *på skolen*, *på universitetet*, *på hospitalet*, *på biblioteket*, *på posthuset*, *på arbejde*, *på café*, *på restaurant*. There's no explainable reason; learn them as a group.

Compare this pair: *at gå **i** skole* (to go to school, as an activity) and *at være **på** skolen* (to be at the school building). The same subtle difference appears in *i seng* (to bed) and *på sengen* (on the bed).
**hos** is only for people: *Jeg er hos lægen* (I'm at the doctor's), *Vi spiser hos Mette*. Using *i* or *på* with people is always wrong.

head: Dansk
English
rows: Kan du vise mig det på kortet?
Can you show me on the map?
Take the first road on the right.
Du kan tage bus nummer fem.
You can take bus number five.

blocks.text: *Jeg er ikke herfra* is a sentence you need to recognize **when you hear it**, because it's an answer you may well get. Another one to recognize: *Det ved jeg desværre ikke.*

blocks.title: You can read Danish street names
items: *-gade* = street in town (Nørregade, Vestergade). *-vej* = a bigger road or one on the edge of town (Amagerbrogade, Ringvej).
*Nørre-* = north, *Søndre-* = south, *Øster-* = east, *Vester-* = west. So *Nørregade* = North Street, and almost every Danish town has all four.
*-borg* = castle, fort, *-havn* = harbor, *-by* = town, *-lund* = grove. *København* literally means "merchants' harbor".
